content:
I have a project using Lean version 4.28 (yes, because aristotle :innocent:) that I want to update to the latest Lean and mathlib version. Would you recommend jumping to 4.33.1 directly or is it better to go step-by-step via 4.29, 4.30, 4.31, etc.? I am unsure because:

  • Doing it step-by-step seems "safer". For example if some mathlib def or lemma is marked as deprecated in 4.29 then there I might still get the information what to replace it with, whereas if in 4.33 it might be completely gone already and thus harder to figure out how to repair a proof.

  • On the other hand, step-by-step might also waste my time if I "repair" a proof to make it work for 4.29, say, but the existing proof would actually work just fine again from 4.30 onwards. Or I might need to repair the same proof multiple times.

Are there best-practices or general opinions about this? I could not really find previous conversations about it.

(And yes, I guess one recommendation would be to "just let Claude figure it out", which I am hesitant to do, but even for that I would want to know whether step-by-step is usually better than jumping versions or not.)

I personally much prefer to update step by step because I get a better sense of what has changed between each version (I bump many projects, not just one, and not necessarily between the same pair of versions), and oftentimes I find a regression that could actually be fixed

Mathlib's deprecation policy is that deprecations stay around for six months, so from that perspective bumping in one go is safe. In practice, there are edge cases (e.g., what if X is renamed to Y, and a new definition X is introduced one version later?), that might make it easier to bump step by step.
The other reason is that a reason for your proof breaking is easier to pinpoint if you know which version upgrade caused it. (On the extreme end, using hopscotch will bisect breaking changes to individual mathlib commits, giving you the maximum amount of context.)

I would just use AI tools to upgrade straight to today's mathlib.

Edit: here's why. After travelling and holidays FLT was about a month behind and I tried using incremental upgrades and it was just too slow and boring, and then I tried using Claude Opus to just bump to modern mathlib and it worked fine. I now have Claude Opus bumping FLT every day to keep it up to date.
It's sometimes a good idea to help the LLM a bit: for example when convert! was introduced Claude didn't know about it, and I found its fixes quite ugly (even if it was able to do the bump).
Telling the LLM to read the bump/v4.X.0 PRs that we land in Mathlib first can be very helpful, so you don't need to tell it by hand (or even know about) the preferred ways to update.
I have just encoutered a proof that breaks when updating Lean step-by-step but keeps working when jumping to 4.33.1 directly. I guess I will jump.
I had tried step-by-step a few weeks ago, but after the recommendations here also went for Claude-assisted jumping. Thanks!
